## README.md

Source: https://github.com/bitsocialnet/spam-blocker/blob/master/README.md

```markdown
# Bitsocial Spam Blocker

Bitsocial Spam Blocker scores posts, replies, and votes for spam risk before a community accepts them. A community installs the challenge package, which sends each publication to a spam blocker service. Low-risk publications pass, high-risk ones are rejected, and the rest are asked to verify with an OAuth sign-in or a CAPTCHA.

This repository is the public integration surface: the challenge package, the shared schemas, and the API contract. The official hosted service at `https://spamblocker.bitsocial.net/api/v1` is closed source and lives in a separate private repository. See [Hosted Spam Blocker Source Policy](./docs/architecture/hosted-service-source-policy.md) for the reasoning.

## Contents

- [Packages](#packages)
- [Quick start](#quick-start)
- [Challenge options](#challenge-options)
- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [Pre-check pass](#pre-check-pass)
- [API contract](#api-contract)
- [Risk scoring and enforcement](#risk-scoring-and-enforcement)
- [Privacy](#privacy)
- [Known limitations](#known-limitations)
- [Development](#development)
- [License](#license)

## Packages

| Package                                                     | Path                 | License            | Purpose                                                               |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`@bitsocial/spam-blocker-challenge`](./packages/challenge) | `packages/challenge` | `GPL-3.0-or-later` | pkc-js challenge that community owners install                        |
| [`@bitsocial/spam-blocker-shared`](./packages/shared)       | `packages/shared`    | `MIT`              | Zod schemas and response types shared by the challenge and the server |

## Quick start

Install the challenge on the Bitsocial server that runs your community:

```bash
bitsocial challenge install @bitsocial/spam-blocker-challenge
```

Enable it on a community:

```bash
bitsocial community edit your-community.bso '--settings.challenges[0].name' @bitsocial/spam-blocker-challenge
```

That uses the hosted service and the default thresholds. The hosted service is the recommended setup because its history across communities is what makes ban-evasion and linked-account detection possible. `serverUrl` stays configurable for any service that implements the [API contract](#api-contract).

To set options, pass them in the same command. All option values are strings.

```bash
bitsocial community edit your-community.bso \
  '--settings.challenges[0].name' @bitsocial/spam-blocker-challenge \
  '--settings.challenges[0].options.autoAcceptThreshold' '0.2' \
  '--settings.challenges[0].options.autoRejectThreshold' '0.8' \
  '--settings.challenges[0].options.countryBlacklist' 'RU,CN,KP' \
  '--settings.challenges[0].options.blockVpn' 'true' \
  '--settings.challenges[0].options.blockTor' 'true'
```

The equivalent community settings, with pkc-js `exclude` rules to skip the check for trusted authors:

```json
{
    "challenges": [
        {
            "name": "@bitsocial/spam-blocker-challenge",
            "options": {
                "serverUrl": "https://spamblocker.bitsocial.net/api/v1",
                "autoAcceptThreshold": "0.2",
                "autoRejectThreshold": "0.8",
                "countryBlacklist": "RU,CN,KP",
                "blockVpn": "true",
                "blockTor": "true"
            },
            "exclude": [{ "role": ["owner", "admin", "moderator"] }, { "postScore": 100 }]
        }
    ]
}
```

## Challenge options

| Option                | Default                                    | Description                                                                 |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `serverUrl`           | `https://spamblocker.bitsocial.net/api/v1` | Spam blocker service URL (`http` or `https`); trailing slashes are stripped |
| `autoAcceptThreshold` | `0.2`                                      | Pass without OAuth or CAPTCHA when the risk score is below this value       |
| `autoRejectThreshold` | `0.8`                                      | Reject when the risk score is at or above this value                        |
| `countryBlacklist`    | _(empty)_                                  | Comma-separated ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country codes to reject, e.g. `RU,CN,KP` |
| `maxIpRisk`           | `1.0`                                      | Reject when the IP risk reported by the service exceeds this value          |
| `blockVpn`            | `false`                                    | Reject publications from VPN IPs                                            |
| `blockProxy`          | `false`                                    | Reject publications from proxy IPs                                          |
| `blockTor`            | `false`                                    | Reject publications from Tor exit nodes                                     |
| `blockDatacenter`     | `false`                                    | Reject publications from datacenter IPs                                     |

Validation:

- Thresholds and `maxIpRisk` must be between 0 and 1, and `autoAcceptThreshold` cannot exceed `autoRejectThreshold`.
- Boolean options accept only `true` or `false`.
- An empty or missing value falls back to the default.
- An unknown country code or any other invalid option makes the challenge throw on every request, so the publication is not accepted.

The country, IP risk, VPN, proxy, Tor, and datacenter rules are applied to the result of `/challenge/verify`, after the user has passed. `blockTor` is also sent to the service so it can reject a Tor connection before asking the user to verify. IP classification is an estimate and can be wrong.

**What is public.** pkc-js strips `options` from the public community record. It publishes only `type`, `description`, `challenge`, and `exclude`. Because `challenge` is the [pre-check marker](#pre-check-pass), the server URL and the Tor-blocking policy (`?blockTor=true`) are public. Thresholds and the other filters stay private to the community operator.

## How it works

1. An author publishes a post, reply, or vote. The community's `getChallenge()` signs an evaluation payload with the community signer and returns a `url/iframe` challenge pointing at `<serverUrl>/iframe/<sessionId>/lazy#payload=...`. No request reaches the service yet.
2. The Bitsocial client asks the author before opening the iframe.
3. Once opened, the iframe posts the signed payload to `/evaluate`. The payload sits in the URL fragment, so it is not sent with the initial iframe request.
4. The service returns a risk score between 0 and 1:
    - below `autoAcceptThreshold`: the session completes;
    - at or above `autoRejectThreshold`: the session fails and the page explains why;
    - in between: the page redirects to the verification page (OAuth sign-in first, CAPTCHA as a fallback).
5. The page tells the client the outcome is ready, and the client sends a `ChallengeAnswer` with an empty string.
6. The community calls `/challenge/verify` with the session id. On success it applies its own IP rules from the options above, then accepts or rejects the publication.

```text
getChallenge() -> lazy iframe URL (no request to the service)
  |
  v
author opens iframe -> POST /evaluate -> riskScore
  |
  ├─ <  autoAcceptThreshold -> completed ----------------------------> /challenge/verify -> success
  ├─ >= autoRejectThreshold -> failed -------------------------------> /challenge/verify -> rejected
  └─ in between -> verification page
        |
        ├─ OAuth sign-in
        |     ├─ enough -> completed --------------------------------> /challenge/verify -> success
        |     └─ not enough -> second OAuth provider, or CAPTCHA
        |
        └─ "I don't have a social account" -> CAPTCHA
              ├─ enough -> completed --------------------------------> /challenge/verify -> success
              └─ not enough -> OAuth required
```

Other behavior of the challenge package:

- `commentEdit`, `commentModeration`, and `communityEdit` requests are accepted locally without contacting the service.
- If the service is unreachable or returns an invalid response during verify, the challenge fails with the error. It never silently accepts or rejects.
- A missing community signer fails the challenge.
- `author.community` in the forwarded request is `undefined` for authors who have never published in the community. The community fills it from its own history.

## Pre-check pass

A client can run a community's spam blocker check before it uploads an attached file, so rejected authors never upload. The community still evaluates the real signed publication, including `link`, when it is published. The pass only lets the community reuse the confirmed user-origin IP and any CAPTCHA or OAuth the author already completed, so the author does not see a second iframe.

### Public marker

The challenge package publishes `community.challenges[i].challenge = "<serverUrl>/precheck"`, for example `https://spamblocker.bitsocial.net/api/v1/precheck`. With `blockTor` enabled the marker is `<serverUrl>/precheck?blockTor=true`. If the community's options are invalid, `challenge` is omitted.

A challenge is pass-capable when its `type` is `"url/iframe"` and `challenge` is an `https` (or localhost `http`) URL whose pathname ends with `/precheck`. Clients accept the `blockTor` parameter and remove it when deriving the API base URL. The server reads the community's published policy independently.

### Obtaining a pass

1. Generate a session id `precheck-<lowercase uuid v4>`.
2. Sign a [pre-check request](#post-precheck) for the draft publication, without `link`, using the author's signer.
3. Open `<serverUrl>/iframe/<sessionId>/precheck#payload=<base64url CBOR>` as a `url/iframe` challenge.
4. After the iframe posts its answer, read `GET <serverUrl>/challenge/status/<sessionId>`.

Only `completed` produces a pass. On `failed`, or if the author closes the check before it finishes, stop before uploading. If the status cannot be read, publish without a pass and let the community check the post as usual.

### Redeeming a pass

After uploading, publish with the pre-check session id as the answer at the index of each pass-capable challenge that applies to the publication. For example, use `challengeRequest: { challengeAnswers: [pass] }` when the spam blocker is `community.challenges[0]`.

Every slot before that index must hold an answer its challenge accepts. Challenges that ignore pre-supplied answers (such as pkc-js `fail`) take any string. A challenge that publishes its own `challenge` text (pkc-js `question`) reads its slot as the author's answer, so do not pre-check a community where such a challenge would receive the pass.

`getChallenge()` looks at its `challengeIndex` for a value matching `^precheck-[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}$` and posts a community-signed `/evaluate` request with `precheckSessionId`. What happens next depends on the returned `status`:

| Result                                             | Community behavior                                                                                      |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `completed` or `failed`                            | Answers immediately through `/challenge/verify`, so its IP, country, and network-type rules still apply |
| `pending`                                          | Returns the usual lazy iframe for the same session, which continues from the pass's CAPTCHA and OAuth   |
| Error, no `status`, or no answer within 10 seconds | Returns the usual lazy iframe, as if no pass was sent                                                   |

A pass is single use and is accepted only for the author signer and community that ran the pre-check.

### Tor-blocking communities

A successful pass still opens a brief lazy iframe when publishing, so the server can check the current connection. Earned CAPTCHA and OAuth credit is kept. This stops an author from passing a pre-check on one network and then publishing through Tor.

Community-side exemptions are unchanged, but a pre-check cannot establish exemptions that depend on another challenge succeeding, such as a whitelist or `.bso` verification. Those authors can see an early Tor rejection even though the community would exempt them.

## API contract

All routes are relative to `serverUrl`, for example `https://spamblocker.bitsocial.net/api/v1`. Response schemas for `/evaluate` and `/challenge/verify` are exported from [`packages/shared/src/types.ts`](./packages/shared/src/types.ts).

| Route                              | Caller                  | Purpose                                             |
| ---------------------------------- | ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `POST /evaluate`                   | Lazy iframe, community  | Score a publication and create its session          |
| `POST /challenge/verify`           | Community               | Read the session outcome and IP intelligence        |
| `POST /precheck`                   | Pre-check iframe        | Score a draft comment before upload                 |
| `GET /challenge/status/:sessionId` | Challenge pages, client | Poll a session's state                              |
| `GET /iframe/:sessionId/lazy`      | Author's browser        | Consent-gated bootstrap page that calls `/evaluate` |
| `GET /iframe/:sessionId/precheck`  | Author's browser        | Bootstrap page that calls `/precheck`               |
| `GET /iframe/:sessionId`           | Author's browser        | Verification page (OAuth and CAPTCHA)               |
| `POST /challenge/complete`         | Verification page       | Submit a solved CAPTCHA                             |
| `GET /oauth/:provider/start`       | Verification page       | Start an OAuth sign-in                              |
| `GET /oauth/:provider/callback`    | OAuth provider          | Finish an OAuth sign-in                             |
| `GET /oauth/status/:sessionId`     | Verification page       | Poll OAuth progress                                 |

### Signed CBOR requests

`/evaluate`, `/challenge/verify`, and `/precheck` take `Content-Type: application/cbor` bodies. CBOR keeps `Uint8Array` values intact, which signature verification depends on. Responses are JSON.

To sign a request, CBOR-encode an object holding the signed properties, sign those bytes with Ed25519, and add:

```typescript
signature: {
    signature: Uint8Array; // Ed25519 signature of the CBOR-encoded signed properties
    publicKey: Uint8Array; // 32-byte Ed25519 public key
    type: "ed25519";
    signedPropertyNames: string[]; // keys of the signed object, in order
}
```

`/evaluate` and `/challenge/verify` are signed by the community signer. This stops parties unrelated to the community from querying the service about its authors. The hosted service checks that the signer matches the community, resolving domain addresses through pkc-js. `/precheck` is signed by the author.

### POST /evaluate

Request:

```typescript
{
    // DecryptedChallengeRequestMessageTypeWithCommunityAuthor from pkc-js.
    // author.community is undefined for first-time publishers.
    challengeRequest: DecryptedChallengeRequestMessageTypeWithCommunityAuthor;
    sessionId?: string; // Caller-generated id for the lazy iframe flow; must not start with "precheck-"
    precheckSessionId?: string; // Pre-check pass being redeemed; must be signed when present
    evaluationOptions?: {
        autoAcceptThreshold?: number;
        autoRejectThreshold?: number;
        blockTor?: boolean; // Community policy; Tor connections are rejected before verification
    };
    timestamp: number; // Unix seconds
    signature: {
        // signedPropertyNames: "challengeRequest" | "sessionId" | "evaluationOptions" | "precheckSessionId" | "timestamp"
    };
}
```

Response:

```typescript
{
    riskScore: number; // 0.0 to 1.0
    explanation?: string; // Human-readable reasoning for the score
    sessionId: string;
    challengeUrl: string; // <serverUrl>/iframe/<sessionId>
    challengeExpiresAt?: number; // Unix seconds, 1 hour after creation
    status?: "pending" | "completed" | "failed"; // Optional so responses from older servers still parse
}
```

The challenge package calls this endpoint directly only to redeem a [pre-check pass](#pre-check-pass). Otherwise the lazy iframe posts the payload after the author opens it. An unusable pass is ignored and never fails the request.

### POST /challenge/verify

Request, signed with the same community signer as the evaluation:

```typescript
{
    sessionId: string;
    timestamp: number; // Unix seconds
    signature: {
        // signedPropertyNames: ["sessionId", "timestamp"]
    }
}
```

Response:

```typescript
{
    success: boolean;
    error?: string; // One-line, user-facing reason when success is false

    // Returned on success so the community can apply its own filters
    ipRisk?: number; // 0.0 to 1.0
    ipAddressCountry?: string; // ISO 3166-1 alpha-2
    challengeType?: string; // e.g. "turnstile"
    ipTypeEstimation?: string; // "residential" | "vpn" | "proxy" | "tor" | "datacenter" | "unknown"
}
```

Completion is tracked on the server. No token passes through the author's client. The community relays `error` to the author. It names the kind of problem in broad terms and never includes scores or thresholds.

### POST /precheck

Called from the author's browser through `/iframe/:sessionId/precheck`. The author identity is the signing public key. `publication.author.address` is untrusted.

Request:

```typescript
{
    sessionId: string; // "precheck-<lowercase uuid v4>", generated by the client
    communityAddress: string; // Domain or IPNS address
    publication: {
        // The comment about to be published, without link, linkWidth, or linkHeight
        author: { address: string; displayName?: string; previousCommentCid?: string };
        content?: string;
        title?: string;
        parentCid?: string;
        postCid?: string;
        spoiler?: boolean;
        nsfw?: boolean;
        flairs?: Flair[];
        timestamp: number; // Unix seconds
    };
    timestamp: number; // Unix seconds, within 5 minutes of server time
    signature: {
        // Author's signer. signedPropertyNames: ["sessionId", "communityAddress", "publication", "timestamp"], all required
    };
}
```

Response:

```typescript
{
    sessionId: string;
    status: "pending" | "completed" | "failed";
    challengeUrl: string;
    challengeExpiresAt: number; // Unix seconds, 1 hour after creation
}
```

The pre-check is not a security boundary. Redemption re-scores the real signed publication, and the community still applies its verify-time rules. Pre-check sessions never count as publishing history. The endpoint is rate-limited per client IP. Repeating a request for an existing session by the same author returns its current state, and any other reuse of the id returns 409.

### GET /challenge/status/:sessionId

Returns `{ completed, status, outcome?, warning? }` and sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, so a client can read a pre-check's result after the cross-origin iframe posts its answer.

- `outcome` explains a rejection, or a verification step that was not enough: `{ code: "blocked" | "rejected" | "more_verification_required", title, message, retryAt? }`.
- `warning` (`{ level: "caution" | "verification_required", title, message }`) appears when many accounts have posted from the author's network.

### Iframe pages

- **`/iframe/:sessionId/lazy`** does not create a session by itself. Its script reads the signed payload from the URL fragment and posts it to `/evaluate`. It then completes, redirects to the verification page, or shows why the publication was rejected until the author presses Close.
- **`/iframe/:sessionId/precheck`** does the same for a `precheck-` session id, posting to `/precheck`.
- **`/iframe/:sessionId`** shows OAuth sign-in buttons. If a CAPTCHA alone can pass at the session's score, it also shows an "I don't have a social account" link. When no OAuth provider is configured, it serves a CAPTCHA only.

Challenge pages post `{ type: "challengeCompletionManaged", sessionId }` to the parent window on load. This tells the client that the page sends the answer itself, as `{ type: "challengeAnswer", challengeAnswers: [""], sessionId }`, once the author has seen the outcome.

The hosted service supports GitHub, Google, Twitter, Yandex, TikTok, Discord, and Reddit sign-in, and Cloudflare Turnstile as the CAPTCHA.

## Risk scoring and enforcement

Everything in this section describes the hosted service, not the challenge package. Fine-grained weights and heuristics are private. See the [source policy](./docs/architecture/hosted-service-source-policy.md).

### Risk score

The score is a weighted combination of account age, karma, author reputation across the network, content and link analysis, publishing velocity, IP intelligence, and linked-signer behavior. Reputation data comes from an indexer that crawls Bitsocial communities and tracks which authors get accepted, removed, or banned.

### Verification credit

Each completed verification step multiplies the risk score. The session passes when the adjusted score drops below the pass threshold (default 0.4).

| Path                                 | Default adjusted score | Passes when the raw score is below |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| One OAuth sign-in                    | score × 0.6            | about 0.67                         |
| CAPTCHA only                         | score × 0.7            | about 0.57                         |
| OAuth + CAPTCHA                      | score × 0.6 × 0.7      | about 0.95                         |
| OAuth + a second, different provider | score × 0.6 × 0.5      | any score that was not rejected    |

A CAPTCHA that is not enough returns `oauthRequired`, and the page goes back to the sign-in view.

### Rate limiting

Before scoring, the service can reject a publication with HTTP 429 when the author exceeds their budget. This stops manual spammers who solve every CAPTCHA.

Base limits, checked per type and then in aggregate:

| Type          | Hourly | Daily   |
| ------------- | ------ | ------- |
| post          | 4      | 20      |
| reply         | 6      | 60      |
| vote          | 10     | 200     |
| **aggregate** | **40** | **250** |

Each limit is multiplied by `ageFactor × reputationFactor`, clamped to 0.25–5.0, and never drops below 1.

| Account age           | `ageFactor` |
| --------------------- | ----------- |
| No history or < 1 day | 0.5         |
| 1–7 days              | 0.75        |
| 7–30 days             | 1.0         |
| 30–90 days            | 1.5         |
| 90–365 days           | 2.0         |
| Over 365 days         | 3.0         |

| Reputation                                  | `reputationFactor` |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| Any ban                                     | 0.5                |
| Removal rate above 30%                      | 0.5                |
| Removal rate 15–30%                         | 0.75               |
| Removal rate below 5% with over 10 comments | 1.25               |
| Otherwise, including no history             | 1.0                |

### Linked accounts on one network

The service links distinct signer public keys first seen on the same confirmed user-origin IP. This makes disposable accounts less useful for evading a community ban, faking a conversation, or voting on related accounts' content.

- The first three signers in a rolling 30-day window are normally treated as one person's devices, because Bitsocial accounts cannot yet sync across devices.
- More signers raise risk progressively. Rapid account churn, ban evasion, repeated failures, or replies and votes between linked signers can require stronger verification.
- Severe or compounded abuse can cause a temporary rejection for the whole network while the evidence stays in the window. Operators can also apply a manual IP block.
- Challenge pages warn authors before their network reaches the limit.

This is a defense local to the hosted service. It is not a protocol-wide identity or ban.

## Privacy

- The hosted operator stores raw IP addresses and publication content for abuse detection. All of it is visible to the operator.
- IP addresses are sent to ipapi.is for classification.
- Communities receive only the country code, the IP risk, the network type estimate, and the pass or fail result. They never receive the raw IP.
- OAuth identities (`provider:userId`) are stored by the operator and never shared with communities. The service only confirms that a sign-in succeeded.
- The `explanation` field gives the reasoning behind a score.

## Known limitations

- IP intelligence is a best-effort estimate and can misclassify VPNs and residential addresses.
- IP options are rejection-only by design. There is no country whitelist or other IP-based auto-approval, because it would be easy to game and could be used to flood a community.
- IP intelligence fields are optional in `/challenge/verify`. The challenge applies an IP rule only when the field it needs is present.
- IP-linked signer clusters are probabilistic. Shared households, offices, and carrier networks can group legitimate users, and attackers can rotate IPs. The allowance and the compound-signal escalation reduce false positives but cannot remove them.

## Development

Requires Node.js 22 or later and Corepack-managed Yarn.

```bash
corepack enable
```

```bash
corepack yarn install
```

| Command                       | What it does                                                |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `corepack yarn build`         | Build `shared`, then `challenge`                            |
| `corepack yarn type-check`    | Type-check both packages                                    |
| `corepack yarn test`          | Run the challenge package's Vitest suite                    |
| `corepack yarn format`        | Format with Prettier                                        |
| `corepack yarn llms:generate` | Regenerate `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt` after doc changes |

```text
packages/
├── challenge/   # @bitsocial/spam-blocker-challenge: getChallenge(), options schema, tests
└── shared/      # @bitsocial/spam-blocker-shared: response schemas and types
docs/
├── architecture/     # Hosted service source policy
└── agent-playbooks/  # Workflow notes for AI agents
```

## docs/architecture/hosted-service-source-policy.md

Source: https://github.com/bitsocialnet/spam-blocker/blob/master/docs/architecture/hosted-service-source-policy.md

```markdown
# Hosted Spam Blocker Source Policy

This decision records why Bitsocial publishes the spam blocker's integration surface while keeping the official hosted service implementation private.

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-12

## Decision

Bitsocial uses a public-integration, private-service model for its official hosted spam blocker.

The following surfaces remain public:

- the community challenge package;
- shared request and response schemas;
- the hosted service's API contract;
- high-level descriptions of risk signals and user-visible enforcement;
- documentation of what information the hosted service processes and exposes to communities.

The following surfaces remain private:

- the official hosted server implementation;
- fine-grained scoring weights, compound abuse heuristics, and operational thresholds that are not part of a user-facing guarantee;
- cross-community abuse analytics and operator investigation tooling;
- deployment, monitoring, and other service-operation details.

The public challenge package keeps `serverUrl` configurable so a community can use a compatible independent service. Compatibility with the public contract does not imply distribution of the official hosted implementation.

## Context

Bitsocial is an open protocol, but the official spam blocker is an optional centralized service. Centralized history lets the service detect patterns that a single community cannot observe reliably, including signer churn, ban evasion, coordinated accounts, and other cross-community abuse.

Publishing the integration contract is necessary for interoperability, independent implementations, and informed use. Publishing the complete adaptive abuse engine is not currently necessary for those goals and would disclose implementation details that can reduce the cost of testing evasion strategies. Keeping the service private also preserves the option for Bitsocial Forge to fund its operation through a managed offering while the long-term business model is still developing.

## Security Position

Private source code is not a primary security control. The hosted service must remain defensible even when attackers understand its endpoints and high-level design. Its security should rely on measures such as authenticated requests, strict validation, rate limiting, infrastructure-level denial-of-service protection, least privilege, monitoring, and responsive abuse operations.

Implementation confidentiality is an additional source of attacker friction, particularly for adaptive scoring and Sybil-detection logic. It must not be used to conceal user-affecting policies, data handling, or the existence of enforcement mechanisms. Those remain documented publicly at the level needed for informed participation and operator accountability.

## Why This Boundary

This model provides:

- **Interoperability:** communities and alternative services can integrate through public packages and schemas.
- **Transparency:** users can understand the categories of evidence, possible enforcement, and relevant data handling.
- **Abuse resistance:** the hosted operator does not publish every implementation detail needed to optimize attacks against the current engine.
- **Operational sustainability:** Bitsocial Forge retains flexibility to offer a managed anti-spam service without making it a protocol requirement.

## Reconsideration Triggers

This decision should be reviewed when one or more of the following becomes true:

1. Significant community demand emerges for a self-hostable official server.
2. A contributor and security-review community exists that can materially improve and maintain the implementation.
3. The service's defensible value has shifted from implementation details to data, operations, reliability, or support.
4. A sustainable open-core model is defined, such as a public reference server with the hosted adaptive risk engine and shared abuse intelligence remaining private.
5. Keeping the implementation private begins to impede protocol adoption, trustworthy independent review, or community choice more than it helps abuse resistance and sustainability.

Any future change should be deliberate, include a license review, separate secrets and production data from source, and preserve compatibility with the public integration contract.
```

---

## AGENTS.md

Source: https://github.com/bitsocialnet/spam-blocker/blob/master/AGENTS.md

```markdown
# AGENTS.md

## Purpose

This file defines the always-on rules for AI agents working on Bitsocial Spam Blocker.
Use it as the default policy. Load linked playbooks only when their trigger condition applies.

## Surprise Handling

Report unexpected repository-specific behavior and continue independent work. Ask only when missing information prevents a correct decision.
After confirmation, add a concise note to `docs/agent-playbooks/known-surprises.md` if the issue is likely to recur.

## Project Overview

Public integration surface for the Bitsocial spam blocker. This repo contains the challenge package and shared schemas used by communities and by the hosted server implementation.

## Instruction Priority

1. User request
2. MUST rules
3. SHOULD rules
4. Playbooks

## Agent Operating Principles

- Before editing, state important assumptions when the task is ambiguous. Ask instead of silently choosing between materially different interpretations.
- Prefer the smallest implementation that solves the requested problem. Do not add speculative abstractions, configurability, or features.
- Keep diffs surgical. Do not refactor, reformat, rename, or "improve" adjacent code unless it is necessary for the task.
- Clean up only artifacts created by the current change, such as newly unused imports or dead helper code.
- For non-trivial work, define success criteria and verify them with the narrowest reliable checks before marking the task complete.

## LLM Knowledge Base Policy

Use compiled context for orientation, not as source of truth.

Source of truth:

- Code, tests, package manifests, docs, and runtime/live evidence when relevant.

Compiled context:

- `AGENTS.md`, directory-specific `AGENTS.md` files, `CLAUDE.md`, and repo-managed `.codex/` and `.claude/` workflow files.
- `docs/agent-playbooks/**`, `docs/agent-runs/**`, `docs/agent-playbooks/known-surprises.md`, and tracked `llms.txt` / `llms-full.txt` files when present.

Agents may use compiled context to navigate quickly, but must verify against source files before making behavioral claims or edits. External code graph, RAG, MCP, or wiki tools are optional local accelerators unless the developer explicitly asks to make one part of the committed workflow.

## Task Router

| Situation                                                              | Action                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Bug reported                                                           | Apply the Testing rules below before editing                                                                           |
| `package.json` changed                                                 | Run `corepack yarn install` to keep `yarn.lock` in sync                                                                |
| Code or automation changed                                             | Select affected checks using `docs/agent-playbooks/verification.md`                                                    |
| New testable behavior added                                            | Add focused Vitest coverage                                                                                            |
| Shared schema changed                                                  | Keep it in `packages/shared`                                                                                           |
| README drifts from implementation                                      | Update `README.md`                                                                                                     |
| Public docs or AI context changed                                      | Run `corepack yarn llms:generate`; inspect and commit any resulting changes to `llms*.txt` so LLM indexes stay current |
| AI workflow files changed                                              | Edit shared sources; run `ai-workflow:sync`, `ai-workflow:check`, and `ai-workflow:test`                               |
| Bug fix or substantive review correction exposes a preventable mistake | Use [retro](.agents/skills/retro/SKILL.md) before finishing; preserve review-only scope.                               |
| Durable resumption or handoff needed                                   | Use `docs/agent-playbooks/long-running-agent-workflow.md`                                                              |
| GitHub operation needed                                                | Use `gh` CLI, not GitHub MCP                                                                                           |
| User-facing UI text                                                    | Use `Bitsocial` for product/network text and `PKC` / `pkc-js` for protocol-core names                                  |

## Stack

- Runtime: Node.js v22+ / TypeScript / ESM
- Workspace: Yarn 4 workspaces (`challenge`, `shared`)
- Public packages: challenge integration / shared Zod schemas
- Tooling: vitest / esbuild / Prettier / commitlint / husky

## Project Structure

```text
packages/
├── challenge/  # package for community owners
└── shared/     # shared types and Zod schemas
```

## MUST Rules

### Environment & Build

- Node.js v22+ required for all packages.
- Prefer Corepack-managed Yarn for install and verification commands.
- Select affected verification using `docs/agent-playbooks/verification.md`; run full build/type-check/tests for runtime integration changes and releases.
- The challenge package runs in Node.js only, never in the browser.
- Prefer static imports; dynamic imports should not be needed.

### Code Style

- Function parameters should use a single object shape: `{param1, param2}`.
- Keep types precise; use `unknown` and narrow guards at external boundaries. Ask only when the underlying contract cannot be established.
- In user-facing UI text, use `Bitsocial` for product/network text and `PKC` / `pkc-js` for protocol-core names.

### Testing

- A bug fix requires either a reproduction of the reported behavior or conclusive source/runtime evidence that identifies both the defect and the correct fix with equivalent certainty.
- If the bug cannot be reproduced and the evidence is not conclusive, do not guess or make speculative changes. Report what was checked, say that the bug was not reproduced, and ask for the missing reproduction details when useful.
- When proceeding from conclusive evidence without a reproduction, explain why the evidence is sufficient and add a targeted regression test when practical.
- Add Vitest coverage for non-trivial, testable behavior changes; keep fixtures focused.
- When a bug is reproduced in a test, confirm the test fails before the fix and passes afterward.

### Dependencies & Types

- Do not duplicate `pkc-js` schemas or types. Import them from `@pkcprotocol/pkc-js`.
- `community.address` can be a domain. Resolve it with `pkc-js` to get the public key.

### Shared Code

- Schemas shared between the challenge package and the private hosted server belong in `packages/shared`.

### Security & Trust

- Author fields are user-provided and not trusted, except `author.community`, which is generated by the community and can be trusted.
- Authors can spam with different signers; the protocol is pseudonymous.

### Git Worktrees

- Always give a new worktree a descriptive name that reflects the task (e.g. `fix-challenge-timeout`, not `wt1`, `tmp`, `feature`, or a numbered slug), so it can be identified at a glance in a long list of worktrees.

## SHOULD Rules

- Keep `README.md` in sync with implementation changes when committing.

## Playbooks

Consult these only when the task touches their domain:

| Topic                      | Location                                              |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| Hooks setup                | `docs/agent-playbooks/hooks-setup.md`                 |
| Skills and tools           | `docs/agent-playbooks/skills-and-tools.md`            |
| Bug investigation workflow | `docs/agent-playbooks/bug-investigation.md`           |
| Long-running task handoff  | `docs/agent-playbooks/long-running-agent-workflow.md` |
| Known surprises log        | `docs/agent-playbooks/known-surprises.md`             |
| Full API spec              | `README.md`                                           |

## Workflow and ownership

- Continue authorized work through implementation, affected checks, and fixes. Ask only when missing information changes the result or an action lacks authorization; do not add approval gates from suggested skill procedures.
- Verify technical claims against source, tests, manifests, and runtime evidence. Agent instructions and generated context orient the task; they do not establish behavior.
- Keep changes scoped, preserve unrelated edits and preexisting artifacts, and stage only task-owned changes. Commit, push, publish, or merge only within the user’s authorization; existing authorization persists.
- Keep `master` releasable. Use a short-lived descriptive `codex/` branch for new work unless the user requests another branch or direct work on `master`. Use separate worktrees for unrelated concurrent tasks; never switch branches underneath another agent.
- Delegate substantial independent slices when useful, with explicit scope, file ownership, acceptance criteria, and evidence to return. Small or coupled work can stay local. Use built-in worker/explorer roles where available; custom roles cover project-specific review or verification.
- One owner runs installs, full suites, builds, and browsers. Parallelize independent reads and non-overlapping edits; use at most four workers by default. Do not run Git cleanup, installs, full verification, or review loops from lifecycle hooks.
- Review the final diff and use the narrowest reliable checks in [verification.md](docs/agent-playbooks/verification.md). Repeat checks only after relevant changes, failures, or new uncertainty. Preserve explicit CI/release requirements.

## Shared AI tooling

- Edit `.agents/skills/` and `.agents/roles/`, then run `corepack yarn ai-workflow:sync`, `corepack yarn ai-workflow:check`, and `corepack yarn ai-workflow:test`.
- `.agents/roles/` is this repository’s generator input, not a native app discovery path. Commit the generated `.codex/agents/*.toml`, `.claude/agents/*.md`, and `.claude/skills/` outputs. Codex reads `.agents/skills/`; Claude uses the generated copies and `CLAUDE.md` importing `AGENTS.md`.
- Leave model and reasoning fields unset in skills and roles. Runtime invocation, app/user defaults, and parent inheritance select them. Do not pin a generation or model family in repository prompts.
- Keep hook schemas and permissions native to each harness; similar file contents do not imply identical runtime behavior. See [skills-and-tools.md](docs/agent-playbooks/skills-and-tools.md).
- Keep skill descriptions precise and roots short. Load references when relevant; preserve domain constraints and supported manual-invocation metadata. Prefer installed tools and current official documentation when versions matter; search for or install additional skills only when requested.
```

## packages/challenge/README.md

Source: https://github.com/bitsocialnet/spam-blocker/blob/master/packages/challenge/README.md

```markdown
# @bitsocial/spam-blocker-challenge

A Bitsocial challenge plugin that protects communities from spam by evaluating publication risk scores and optionally presenting an interactive challenge to users.

## Using Spam Blocker In Your Community

Community owners add the spam blocker challenge to their community settings. When enabled, user-generated publications return a consent-gated iframe URL. The Bitsocial Spam Blocker server evaluates the publication only after the user opens that iframe. Low-risk publications complete immediately after evaluation, high-risk publications are rejected, and medium-risk publications continue into an interactive iframe challenge. Community-level actions (`commentEdit`, `commentModeration`, and `communityEdit`) are accepted locally because they do not require spam detection.

First install the challenge on the Bitsocial server:

```bash
bitsocial challenge install @bitsocial/spam-blocker-challenge
```

Then set it on your community with one command:

```bash
bitsocial community edit your-community.bso '--settings.challenges[0].name' @bitsocial/spam-blocker-challenge
```

That uses the hosted Bitsocial Spam Blocker server and the default thresholds. This is the strongly recommended configuration because the centralized service can correlate cross-community abuse and signer clusters over time.

The hosted service normally allows up to three signer public keys on a confirmed user-origin IP during its rolling window, accommodating users who cannot yet sync a Bitsocial signer across devices. Excessive account switching, rapid signer churn, ban evasion, or interactions between linked signers can trigger stronger verification or a temporary IP-level rejection. This policy is enforced by the hosted server, not by the public challenge package itself.

To customize thresholds or IP-based rejection rules, pass options in the same command:

```bash
bitsocial community edit your-community.bso \
  '--settings.challenges[0].name' @bitsocial/spam-blocker-challenge \
  '--settings.challenges[0].options.autoAcceptThreshold' '0.2' \
  '--settings.challenges[0].options.autoRejectThreshold' '0.8' \
  '--settings.challenges[0].options.countryBlacklist' 'RU,CN,KP' \
  '--settings.challenges[0].options.blockVpn' 'true' \
  '--settings.challenges[0].options.blockTor' 'true'
```

All option values should be strings.

## Configuration

You can also open your community settings interactively:

```bash
bitsocial community edit
```

Then add or edit the `challenges` array in your community settings to include the spam blocker challenge with your desired options.

## Options

| Option                | Default                                    | Description                                                                          |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `serverUrl`           | `https://spamblocker.bitsocial.net/api/v1` | URL of a compatible spam blocker service; the official hosted service is recommended |
| `autoAcceptThreshold` | `0.2`                                      | Complete verification after iframe evaluation when risk is below this value          |
| `autoRejectThreshold` | `0.8`                                      | Reject after iframe evaluation when risk is above this value                         |
| `countryBlacklist`    | _(empty)_                                  | Comma-separated ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country codes to block (e.g. `RU,CN,KP`)          |
| `maxIpRisk`           | `1.0`                                      | Reject if IP risk score exceeds this threshold (estimation only)                     |
| `blockVpn`            | `false`                                    | Reject publications from VPN IPs (estimation only)                                   |
| `blockProxy`          | `false`                                    | Reject publications from proxy IPs (estimation only)                                 |
| `blockTor`            | `false`                                    | Reject publications from Tor exit nodes (estimation only)                            |
| `blockDatacenter`     | `false`                                    | Reject publications from datacenter IPs (estimation only)                            |

## How It Works

1. When a user publishes a post, reply, or vote to a community, the challenge signs the publication locally and returns a lazy iframe URL. `getChallenge()` does not call `/evaluate`.
2. The Bitsocial client asks the user before opening the spam blocker iframe.
3. After the user opens the iframe, the iframe sends the signed payload to `/evaluate`. This is the first spam blocker server evaluation request for the publication.
4. The server returns a **risk score** between 0 and 1:
    - **Below `autoAcceptThreshold`**: Verification completes immediately.
    - **Above `autoRejectThreshold`**: Verification fails immediately.
    - **Between thresholds**: The iframe presents OAuth and/or CAPTCHA verification.
5. After challenge verification, the server's `/challenge/verify` endpoint confirms whether the user passed. Additional IP-based policies (country, VPN, proxy, Tor, datacenter blocking) are applied if configured.
6. Community-level actions (`commentEdit`, `commentModeration`, and `communityEdit`) are accepted without calling `/evaluate`.
7. The challenge publishes `<serverUrl>/precheck` as its public `challenge` so clients can run the spam blocker before uploading a file. A client that completed that pre-check sends its `precheck-<uuid>` session id as this challenge's answer in `challengeRequest.challengeAnswers`; `getChallenge()` then redeems it with `/evaluate` server-to-server and answers without a second iframe when the session is already decided. If redemption is still pending or fails, the usual lazy iframe is returned. See the repository README's pre-check pass section for the client flow.

## License

`@bitsocial/spam-blocker-challenge` is licensed under `GPL-3.0-or-later`. See [`LICENSE`](./LICENSE).
```

# @bitsocial/spam-blocker-shared

## docs/agent-playbooks/known-surprises.md

Source: https://github.com/bitsocialnet/spam-blocker/blob/master/docs/agent-playbooks/known-surprises.md

```markdown
# Known Surprises

Use this file for repo-specific surprises that are likely to recur.

## Starter Notes

- Existing SQLite databases will not gain new columns automatically because the schema uses `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`.
- Risk-score scenario output is derived from the current scoring model; update the docs and regenerate it together when factors change.
- The server is Node-only. Browser tooling is only for challenge iframe verification, not for running the server.
```

## docs/agent-playbooks/long-running-agent-workflow.md

Source: https://github.com/bitsocialnet/spam-blocker/blob/master/docs/agent-playbooks/long-running-agent-workflow.md

```markdown
# Long-running work

Use durable state only when a task needs resumption or handoff. Short tasks and ordinary delegation do not require a task board.

Record scope, acceptance criteria, important decisions, file/branch ownership, completed checks, failures, and the next concrete step in `docs/agent-runs/<descriptive-slug>/progress.md` when shared tracked state is useful. Add a feature list only when multiple independent outcomes need tracking; templates live in `templates/`.

On resumption, inspect the current diff and relevant source before acting. Reuse verification for unchanged work and run only affected checks after new edits. Do not start a dev server or install dependencies solely to update the handoff.
```

## docs/agent-playbooks/bug-investigation.md

Source: https://github.com/bitsocialnet/spam-blocker/blob/master/docs/agent-playbooks/bug-investigation.md

```markdown
# Bug Investigation

Use this playbook when the user reports a bug or a regression.

## Minimum Sequence

1. Inspect the affected files and surrounding code.
2. Check recent git history for the affected area.
3. Reproduce the bug with a test case first when possible.
4. Make the smallest fix that addresses the observed behavior.
5. Re-run the relevant verification commands.

## Practical Guidance

- Prefer `git log --oneline -5 -- <file>` or `git blame` before editing.
- Keep the investigation scoped to the reported behavior.
- If a schema or DB behavior is implicated, confirm whether the on-disk database needs to be recreated.
```

## docs/agent-playbooks/skills-and-tools.md

Source: https://github.com/bitsocialnet/spam-blocker/blob/master/docs/agent-playbooks/skills-and-tools.md

```markdown
# Skills and tools

Shared source files avoid hand-maintained copies while preserving each app’s native discovery paths.

| Content              | Edited source                                 | App-loaded output                                                                                                             |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Skills               | `.agents/skills/<name>/`                      | Codex uses this path; Claude uses generated `.claude/skills/<name>/` copies.                                                  |
| Custom agents        | `.agents/roles/<name>.md`                     | Generated `.codex/agents/<name>.toml` and `.claude/agents/<name>.md`.                                                         |
| Project instructions | `AGENTS.md` and scoped directory instructions | Codex reads `AGENTS.md`; `CLAUDE.md` imports `@AGENTS.md` for Claude. Existing nested CLAUDE.md imports remain where present. |
| Hooks                | Shared formatter and native entrypoints       | `.codex/hooks.json` and `.claude/settings.json`.                                                                              |

`.agents/roles` is a repository-specific generator schema, not an app standard. Its supported fields are `name`, `description`, and optional `sandbox-mode`. No repository field selects models or reasoning effort; runtime invocation, configured defaults, or parent inheritance decide. This does not promise automatic selection of the best current model.

Read-only roles map to Codex `sandbox_mode` and Claude tool restrictions. These controls have different semantics; Claude's Bash availability is not an OS sandbox. Parent assignments still define scope.

After editing sources, run `corepack yarn ai-workflow:sync`, `corepack yarn ai-workflow:check`, and `corepack yarn ai-workflow:test`. Review and commit generated outputs together. Sync does not silently delete obsolete files; remove obsolete task-owned outputs explicitly and let validation detect drift. Skills are portable copies, not symlinks.

Keep descriptions short and discriminating; place conditional procedures in linked references. Preserve domain-specific requirements rather than copying another product’s policy. Avoid compulsory agent chains, full tests for wording edits, unconditional external skill installs, and extra approval gates. Built-in worker/explorer roles handle general implementation; retained custom agents cover concrete independent review or domain tasks.

Official references, checked 2026-09-12: [Codex skills](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills), [Codex subagents](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents), [Claude skills](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills), [Claude subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents), and [Claude imports](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory). Generator/schema checks are separate from live app discovery and delegation tests.

Maintenance approach: [OpenAI’s guidance on skills and prompts for GPT-6 Astra](https://developers.openai.com/blog/rethinking-skills-and-prompts-for-gpt-6-astra). Keep useful guidance for other contributors and models while reducing redundant workflow instructions.
```
